title: Industrial Gamma Radiation Signals: An Untapped Resource to Reconstruct Neogene Paleoclimate Off Northwest Australia
content:
Abstract

Paleoceanographic reconstructions require both high-resolution temporal records and high-density spatial coverage. Scientific drilling provides detailed paleoclimate time-series, but its spatial distribution limits our ability to capture regional climate dynamics. Industrial drilling data, particularly natural gamma radiation (NGR) records, offer an opportunity to bridge this spatio-temporal gap. In this study, we analyze wireline downhole-logging NGR measurements from the South Galapagos-1 industrial well in the Browse Basin, offshore Northwest Australia. The upper portion of this industry site corresponds to the Neogene system, tracks Milanković-driven climate variability, and provides a continuous archive of regional paleoclimate evolution since 21.5 Ma. Using astronomical tuning, we establish a robust age-depth model that aligns the South Galapagos-1 NGR record with the global δ18O benthic isotope climate-stratigraphic backbone. Our results reveal a shift in Northwest Australia's climate response to global-climate forcing around ∼12.7 Ma, coinciding with the expansion of the Antarctic ice sheet. Before this transition, NGR peaks correspond to arid phases of Australian desert expansion during globally-colder intervals. After 12.7 Ma, however, NGR peaks instead reflect wetter conditions, indicating intensified Australian monsoon activity during globally-warmer periods. This shift is attributed to astronomically-driven biome changes that influenced the transport of detrital material from land to sea, further shaped by tectonic reconfigurations of the Indonesian Throughflow and variations in Indo-Pacific Walker circulation patterns. Therewith, our study highlights the potential of industrial NGR data as a paleoclimate proxy, helping to fill both geographic and stratigraphic gaps left by scientific drilling.
